This is where a signal is modiﬁed in an unwanted way by a variety of di↵erent factors. We see examples of it when a TV signal is poor and parts of the image don’t show and when audio contains white noise such as when you rip a CD that has been scratched so cannot be copied completely correctly. Noise means a signal is less e�cient as it is carrying information that is not required and it makes it more di�cult to decode the message at the other end of the system. Digital transmission is a way of reducing noise as we know that the transmitted is either 0 or 1, transmitted at certain frequencies and if we receive frequencies that aren’t the two we are expecting, we can make a good guess at which one is supposed to be received. However, there is still some guessing and we cannot be certain that we have decoded the message correctly. As a result, we would like to keep noise to a minimum as eradicating it completely is highly unlikely. 3.2.1 How do we represent a Noisy Channel? Firstly, we need to consider how to write down this noisy channel that we are dealing with. We need to be aware that we don’t know where the noise has come from, it could be either transducer or from the transmission in the middle, or a combination of the two. So the received signal may not be the same as the one that was sent from the transmitter. We can break this down into two cases, the ﬁrst is that a particular transmitted signal is always a↵ected by noise in the same way, so we can deﬁne a deﬁnite function for the received signal from the transmitted signal. Once Claude Shannon had written his paper, Information Theory as a ﬁeld of study was born. Shannon laid the groundwork for digital communications, some- thing we take for granted today. His paper had such a profound e↵ect and gained such a following in a short space of time that in 1956, Shannon wrote a paper called The Bandwagon.In this paper, he seemed to lament how popular Informa- tion Theory had become and how people had used the information he published. Shannon felt that people applied the maths without proper consideration of how they had actually applied it, especially in subject areas outside of the mathematics of communication, where the maths had been aimed. However, Shannon had provided the basis for a lot of breakthroughs that we will look at in more detail in this section. 6.1 Data Compression Does this link to Numerical Methods with the interpolation Q on Assignment 2 Sem 1?? studentr page 151. Data compression is a huge part of our every day lives, from CD’s to digi- tal radio to the signals our TV’s receive. In this section we will consider audio compression as it is simpler but the ideas can be expanded into the 4-dimension video compression as well. The basic idea of compression is that we can carry the same amount of data but using a smaller bandwidth or that we can carry data a lot more quickly using the same size of bandwidth. It is clear why this is a beneﬁt as it will save money on the bandwidth required or on the amount of data transmitted. The compression factor is a way of measuring how much bandwidth we are saving. Deﬁnition 6.1.1. The compression factor is the ratio between the source data rate and the channel data rate. [9] Data Inlet Compressor /Encoder Channel Expander /Decoder Data Sink 10 Figure 2. A basic data compression system. [9] There are two types of coding, both with their own merits. Deﬁnition 6.1.2. Lossless Coding is where the data that the decoder outputs and the initial input data from the data inlet are identical bit for bit. Lossless coding is very good for computer programs as if one bit is incorrect, such as missing one semi colon in a C++ program, the whole code won’t work. It does mean that the compression factor cannot generally go above 2:1 so it is not always the cheapest option and if we can a↵ord to lose some of the data, lossy coding will be used. Deﬁnition 6.1.3. Lossy Coding is compression where the data from the decoder and the initial data are not the same bit for bit. [9] Lossy coding is predominantly used in compressing audio and video data. In audio, some frequencies can be lost if there are enough other frequencies in the audio data that make it di�cult for the human ear to detect the loss. This sort of coding is called perceptive and requires a model of the human senses that is fairly accurate. In order to save more time and therefore money, we can make decoders that remember the signals that have gone before and can use that to generate some of the current signal. This means that the transmitter doesn’t need to transmit part of the signal. In theory, you only need to send the entropy of a signal as it is the only unexpected and unpredictable part of the signal but in practice, this isn’t possible due to noise, loss of signal over distance and other factors that mean the quality of signal is lost and that we would be missing bits o the signal after decoding. It is worth noting, however, that compressed data is more susceptible to corruption and errors as the redundant code is removed (that which we can calculate from what has gone before) and this is what makes a code resistant to errors. 6.2 Digitisation 6.3 ARPANET 6.4 Internet 11
